description: We’re a student team taking part in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and working on the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. We’re combining programming, science, and design to build our own approach to the challenge and make lunar mission information easier to explore and understand.
summary: We made a simulation game for moving between the earth and the moon. Coordinates can be entered to go to that point on the moon or earth. We address the challenge by creating a fun and engaging game like atmosphere for anyone who may not have prior astronomy knowledge to learn new things without it seeming boring or overwhelming. This is important as to bring advancement towards any field there must be sufficient nurturing of talents.
details: Our project is a moon landing simulator, it takes in 3 coordinates, the starting earth coordinates, the moon landing coordinates, and the returning earth coordinates. Along with this the starting date of the launch is asked in the format SPICE functions need to calculate positions for the earth, moon and sun. Through this information we were able to calculate the trajectory a ship might take to reach these points. The duration for the flight can be set from the script, but it is 72 hours for the travel to the moon and another 72 for the return journey. The draw trajectory button also gives a lot of extra data which also includes if illumination reaches that are of the moon when the ship reaches the coordinates. The simulation button allows you to see the actual journey of the rocket from the earth to the moon and back. Coordinates can be entered to go to specific parts of the earth or moon. if certain popular coordinates are chosen then the user gets a special message, this promotes curiosity among anyone playing. The controls are kept simple for ease of access, R to orbit earth, E to orbit the ship and F to focus on the current selected object, clicking on any object selects it, that way the sun and moon can also be orbit in some situations. Since there are already many sophisticated and well-developed lunar simulation applications we decided to take a different approach to things. Instead of specializing data and aiming for utmost precision we want to have a sense of simplicity and stimulation to revolve around our game. That way we can introduce it to audiences who may not have much knowledge or interest in astronomy. This will engage them without confusing them with in depth parameters, it eases their understanding of such concepts by slowly showing things at their own pace, all advanced parameters are only accessible through a panel and only the basics are present at surface. With this hopefully we can inspire others and let them discover their fascination for space and its incomprehensible infinity. We used unity as our game engine, C# as our programming language, and a Alienware m16 r2 to create the game. Spice was wrapped into a DLL so that it could be used in Unity. We think our projects art style and game-like sound effects will engage users more than what a bland or more professional simulator might, this would allow complete beginners to develop a deep interest or engagement. Our team considered how the much the advanced information looked like a CLI therefore we animated the text to slowly reveal itself. We also thought that the player should be given a degree of interactive control, so we created movement that was inspired by Kerbel space program, it allowed the player to orbit the celestial body of their choice and to look and the finer details within them. We thought as for how we could display a rocket trajectory as simply as possible and finalized with the design choice of keeping a simple curved line showing only the path to and from the moon.
